messages.subject: [statnet_help] creating an attribute similarity/difference matrix
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a simple procedure question.  I've been doing network regressions
both with 'netlm' and 'netlogit' as implemented in 'sna.'  In both cases
some of the independent variables I've been using are symmetric matrices
constructed on the basis of either nodal attribute similarities or absolute
differences between node pairs.  In UCINET the creation of these matrices is
quite simple (with the 'from attribute to matrix' routine under the 'data'
manipulations menu).  I was wondering if there is a way of creating matrices
like these within statnet/sna (either from the attributes embedded in a
network object, or a vector object that contains the attribute values) so
that I don't have to import them from UCINET every time (which is what I've
been doing!).  If available, a syntax example would be much appreciated!

 

In advance, thanks!

 

Jorge M Rocha

EGADE Business School

 

 

 

Description: firma smaller

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM with Endogenous Terms
messages.body_plain:
Dear Statnet Community,

If I estimate an ERGM model that does NOT include endogenous network  
terms (e.g., isolates, mutual, triangle) and ONLY includes exogenous  
covariates (e.g., nodecov, dyadcov), then the reported ERGM results  
include the ordinary coefficient/standard error BUT do NOT include a  
MCMC standard errors.

My question: Are the reported standard errors corrected for the dyadic  
dependence that is inherent in the network data?  If YES, then what  
statistical model is used to correct them?  (An article citation here  
would be most welcome.)  If NO, then is there any way to ask the ERGM  
routine to run the MCMC simulation WITHOUT including endogenous  
parameters?

Thanks in advanced for any help.

Best,

Michael

--

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM with Endogenous Terms
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

The answer is no.  If your model does not include dyadic dependent terms, 
then it is not necessary to use MCMC for the estimation, so there is no 
MCMC related SE.

If you believe there is dyadic dependence in the network, then you will 
need to represent this in the model -- by using a term (or terms) that 
captures the dependence.  What do you mean by "inherent dependence"?

best,
Martina

gd(1,3,flomarriage)

gd(1,4,flomarriage

Mark

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM with Endogenous Terms
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michael -

On 10/09/2011 05:12 PM, Michael T. Heaney wrote:
> Dear Statnet Community,
>
> If I estimate an ERGM model that does NOT include endogenous network
> terms (e.g., isolates, mutual, triangle) and ONLY includes exogenous
> covariates (e.g., nodecov, dyadcov), then the reported ERGM results
> include the ordinary coefficient/standard error BUT do NOT include a
> MCMC standard errors.
>

Yes - there is no need for MCMC in this case.  (This is actually a 
network logit model -- see also netlogit in sna.)

> My question: Are the reported standard errors corrected for the dyadic
> dependence that is inherent in the network data?

Is there in fact "inherent" dyadic dependence in your data?  If so, why 
are you fitting an independence model?  (To put it another way, if you 
believe that there is dependence, then you should model it.  The 
reported standard error estimates reflect your modeling assumptions.)

> If YES, then what
> statistical model is used to correct them? (An article citation here
> would be most welcome.) If NO, then is there any way to ask the ERGM
> routine to run the MCMC simulation WITHOUT including endogenous parameters?

The MCMC here is a red herring -- it's just used to perform the 
numerical calculations required to obtain the estimates.  I think you 
want to determine whether you really believe you have an autocorrelation 
problem, and if so model accordingly.

Another option, if you are just interested in hypothesis testing for the 
covariate effects, would be to use either netlogit (w/QAP) in sna or the 
netperm package.  The QAP test for netlogit is not known to have great 
properties, so caveats apply; the netlm case is better behaved.  The 
netperm model can also be used in a similar manner, but is more exotic. 
  In any event, all three provide avenues for estimating relations among 
matrices (and testing hypotheses about the same) while controlling for 
within-matrix autocorrelation.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] ERGM with Endogenous Terms
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michael -

On 10/09/2011 07:28 PM, Michael T. Heaney wrote:
> Dear Martina,
>
> Thanks so much for your quick response.
>
> The problem that I am having is that if I use the endogenous network
> terms, then I am getting errors that say 'Error: cannot allocate vector
> of size 41.5 mb'.
>
> My network has 738 nodes.

What are you putting into the model?  We've fit much larger networks 
(but, of course, a lot depends on the terms you use).

>
> By 'inherent dependence' I mean that since each node appears in the data
> 737 times, I want the standard errors to be computed in a way that
> accounts for the common variance among these 737 observations.
>

The notion of "common variance" is not very helpful here.  How, 
precisely, do you think that the nodes are leading to dependence among 
the dyads?  (There are many ways of thinking about this.)  It sounds 
like you may have in mind sender/receiver effects (i.e., fixed effects 
for rows and/or columns, or "sociality" for both).  This is only one 
form such dependence can take, however -- the Markov graphs represent 
another.

If you were trying to use sender/receiver/sociality terms with a model 
of that size, I imagine you might have run into problems (you are adding 
a vast number of parameters in that case).  If you really think you have 
substantial heterogeneity that can't be captured by degree distribution 
terms (e.g., through gwdegree), then you might want to go the 
permutation test/model route....

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] follow-up question on "structural zeroes"
messages.body_plain:
greetings,

a while ago i had a question about modeling directed two-mode data, and have something of a follow-up about this question. thanks to the guidance steve provided, it seemed that while statnet is not able to model bipartite directed networks, i could basically treat my network as unipartite but include terms in my models for "homophily" within each mode... ergm would then recognize that no within-mode ties existed, fix these parameters at negative infinity, and respect this restriction during parameter estimation.

i have another situation where certain actors are not allowed to contact each other- but these "impossible" ties are not structured in such a way that i can model them with nodematch terms. in other words, they are something like "structural zeroes" in the language of RSiena- and i would like to estimate a model that respects this restriction where some ties are not possible. my first thought was to follow the same approach as above, but instead of using nodematch terms to identify the "impossible" ties, i would do the same thing with an edgecov term. when i run this model, however, ergm does not seem to recognize that these ties are impossible in the same way it does for the nodematch situation... and so instead of getting a parameter that is fixed at negative infinity, i simply get a parameter estimate that is strongly negative (say, -16) and becomes even more strongly negative with each MCMC iteration.

my question, then, is whether this approach is problematic for any reason? or is this actually a reasonable way to impose "structural zeroes" in the model? it seems the ideal case would be to be able to fix this parameter at negative infinity... but if there is not currently a way to do this, i want to make sure the approach i've taken in practice (i.e. letting the edgecov parameter work its way to an unstable, but strongly negative value) is not creating other issues of which i'm unaware. any help would be greatly appreciated! thanks,

-kevin

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Latent Cluster Model with package latentnet
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Alla,

In case this is still of use, constructing a network with a latent
structure and a particular degree sequence requires more than just
latentnet, since latentnet only deals with unconstrained networks.

One way to do this is to use the fact that conditional on the latent
space positions, a latent space model is essentially an ERGM with a
particularly structured dyadic covariate, so you can use the ergm
package to simulate it.

Let y0 be the network object whose degree sequence you want to "copy",
let Zi be the i'th latent position. Then,

1) Construct a covariate matrix with elements Xij=-|Zi-Zj|.
2) Run something along the lines of 
library(ergm)
y <- simulate(y0~edgecov(Xij),theta0=c(1),constraints=~degrees)

Then y should be a realization of a network with the correct degree
sequence and a latent position structure. You might need to use a long
burn-in.

                          I hope this helps,
                          Pavel

messages.subject: [statnet_help] follow-up question on "structural zeroes"
messages.body_plain:
Kevin,

The edgecov term doesn't do the extreme value detection that nodemix
does. We may implement it in the a future release. In the meantime,
enclosing the term in the offset() function, e.g, offset(edgecov(X)),
should fix it at whatever value you specify in theta0.

                   Pavel

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This illustrates a general point that's worth highlighting for all 
users.  Often the way to accomplish a task in statnet is to write a 
(relatively short) piece of R code that is external to statnet itself. 
This is by design.  The great strength of the R platform is the wide 
range of existing functions (both in base and in the packages) that 
allow many ways to accomplish all sorts of tasks.  We wrote statnet in R 
specifically so that users could draw on all of that.  So when you don't 
see the functionality that you might be expecting in statnet, that 
doesn't mean it's necessarily unavailable, especially if it seems like a 
common task that many would want to do. In those cases, it probably 
reflects the fact that the task requires only a small piece of R code, 
so there was really no need to write a new function.  Unlike stand-alone 
network packages, then, there can be extra legwork to do in terms of 
learning more R.  But the upside is that once you do it, you have great 
flexibility.  Not just for network modeling, but for the entire world of 
statistical computing.

That said, this forum remains the perfect place to ask these questions, 
and hear from other users about how they accomplished a task -- whether 
with a statnet function or R code more generally. Or to share your own 
insights about how to accomplish a network-related task with a 
particularly clever bit of R code that you think others might benefit from.

Cheers,
Steve
